claims.text: Toughness retention in high-entropy alloys is governed by the extent of diffusion-driven elemental segregation at grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary segregation promotes the formation of brittle secondary precipitates.
Grain-boundary secondary precipitates reduce resistance to crack propagation and decrease toughness.
The quenched, homogenized baseline has a uniform solid-solution structure with minimal elemental segregation.
Thermal exposure around 700–800 °C is sufficient to activate diffusion in the proposed alloy.
Elevated-temperature diffusion causes specific alloying elements to segregate at grain boundaries.
The segregated grain-boundary regions provide nucleation sites for secondary phases.
Brittle secondary phases accumulate along grain boundaries during aging.
Grain-boundary brittle phases compromise the alloy's ability to absorb energy during deformation.
Thermally aged specimens will have lower room-temperature fracture toughness than the as-quenched baseline.
Aging will increase the concentration or density of secondary precipitates along grain boundaries.
The degree of grain-boundary precipitation will correlate with the magnitude of toughness loss.
The proposed behavior applies when diffusion is appreciable but has not progressed to complete phase separation.
The proposed behavior is expected particularly for compositions containing segregation-prone elements.
Alloys engineered with additives that stabilize grain boundaries against segregation may fall outside the hypothesis's applicability.
Some high-entropy alloy compositions may resist segregation because of compensatory alloying effects.
